# Community guidelines

These community guidelines reflect the values and commitments of Open Source Europe. They aim to create a positive and productive community for all involved.

## Introduction

OSE is committed to keeping a respectful, inclusive, and supportive environment for all its members, participants, and stakeholders. These community guidelines set out how we expect people to behave and interact in our community.

***

## Scope

These community guidelines apply to all individuals participating in OSE activities, including members, partners, volunteers, and attendees at OSE events.

***

## Core principles

* **Transparency**: Operate with transparency and integrity. Ensure that financial activities, decision-making processes, and communications are open and accessible.
* **Respect and dignity**: Treat everyone with respect and dignity. Harassment, discrimination, or exclusionary behavior of any kind will not be tolerated.
* **Inclusivity**: Promote a welcoming environment where diversity is valued. Encourage participation from all individuals regardless of gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, disability, sexual orientation, or age.

***

## Expected behavior

* **Collaboration**: Work together and support each other. Take part constructively and be open to different points of view.
* **Communication**: Communicate respectfully and professionally. Avoid offensive, inflammatory, or inappropriate language.
* **Responsibility**: Take responsibility for your actions and their impact on others. Address conflicts or issues promptly and respectfully.

***

## Unacceptable behavior

* **Harassment**: Any form of harassment, including but not limited to sexual harassment, bullying, or intimidation.
* **Discrimination**: Discriminatory comments or actions based on personal characteristics or beliefs.
* **Disruption**: Intentional disruption of events, meetings, or online forums.

***

## Reporting and enforcement

* **Reporting**: If you witness or experience behavior that violates these community guidelines, report it to the designated contact person immediately.
* **Review and follow-up**: Reports are taken seriously and reviewed to decide the right next steps. OSE does not always run an internal investigation, and it does not guarantee a response time.
* **Consequences**: Individuals who violate these community guidelines may face consequences, including warnings, expulsion from events, or removal from OSE activities.

***

## Safeguarding

OSE is committed to safeguarding the well-being of all participants. See our [Safeguarding policy](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/safeguarding-policy/) for details of our safeguarding practices.

***

## Continuous improvement

We keep improving our policies and practices. We welcome feedback and suggestions to improve this Code of Conduct. You can send them to our team.

***

## Contact information

For questions, concerns, or to report a violation of this Code of Conduct, please contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

# Contact OSE

## Choose the right contact

The following table lists where to go for each kind of question:

| You need help with                                             | What to do                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A submitted expense                                            | Use its comments on Open Collective for routine questions. Send sensitive information privately to OSE. |
| Hosting, a funding arrangement, or another OSE question        | Email <home@opensourceeurope.org>.                                                                         |
| Suspected misuse of funds or an issue involving administrators | Contact OSE directly in private. You do not need to go through those administrators.                    |
| A safeguarding concern                                         | Use the [safeguarding contacts and procedure](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/safeguarding-policy/).        |
| A technical problem with Open Collective                       | Use [platform support](https://opencollective.com/help).                                                |

OSE aims to answer general questions within seven business days. The seven days are a target, not a guaranteed response time. It does not replace the specific guidance for applications, payments, or safeguarding.

## Expense follow-up and sensitive concerns

Use comments on the expense for routine questions about a submitted expense. The comments are not public. The expense submitter, the Collective's administrators, and the fiscal host's administrators can see them. Email <home@opensourceeurope.org> directly for sensitive information that the Collective's administrators should not see.

For suspected misuse of funds or a problem involving Collective administrators, contact the OSE team directly in private at <home@opensourceeurope.org>. You do not need to go through the administrators concerned.

## Internal conflicts

Collectives manage their own internal conflicts. OSE intervenes when the situation affects funds or hosting conditions. It does not promise mediation.

# Mission, vision & impact areas

It all comes back to resilience.

## Mission

Open Source Europe (OSE) works to make the social and solidarity economy and open source technologies sustainable. The OSE mission is to enable initiatives to raise and spend money transparently under a common umbrella nonprofit.

*Open Collective is an unusual company. In its ecosystem, a software company coexists with independent associations and foundations known as 'hosts.' OSE is growing as one of the first major fiscal hosts on the European continent. OSE hosts initiatives that share its values and work toward a better future. The OSE values, and the OSE vision for a healthy and thriving world, start with resilience. From that central concern come six related areas where OSE works to make a difference.*

### Resilient communities

Humanity is divided on countless fronts, but most people agree on the need for resilience. When systems fail, people need fallback buffers. Resilient communities don't break when one system failure causes the next. They have a patchwork of fallbacks to absorb the shocks. Resilience is when people next to you on the street know how to give cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or can swim to save someone from drowning. It is when the families in your neighborhood own their own homes. It is also when your community has enough nurses to deliver your children and enough teachers to educate them. It is when every other house in your neighborhood has solar panels that feed spare capacity back to the grid. When authorities arrive at a natural disaster, they find that the local community has already started helping itself. It is a society of ordinary people who are great leaders when they need to be. Resilience keeps people, jobs, and services in your hometown. When people can trust their community to catch them if they fall, they can safely turn their attention to working for the greater good. That is why OSE puts resilient communities at the center of its mission.

### Open innovation

When people use science and technology wisely, they become more resourceful. They expand their horizons and capabilities. If they share their findings, they grow stronger together. OSE encourages people to work together. Through the network effect, OSE helps knowledge and technology spread faster. Without this sharing, society risks becoming divided by increasing technological gaps. Civil society is key to making innovation available to all. Distributed networks of passionate people around the world develop open source software. Citizen scientists collect and share data. Civil engineers document how to build more energy-efficient homes. Technologists share blueprints for 3D printers and robots. Maker spaces around the world help people innovate and repair. Open innovation makes all of this possible.

### Commons stewardship

When a social innovation, cultural institution, or green space starts to feel like it has always been there, it has become a common good. Ideally, the commons that people create become so readily available that they appear unremarkable. At exactly this point, the common good becomes vulnerable. Humankind longs for what is new and exciting. People want to solve the urgent problems of the day, and that is where they focus their attention. But people also need to maintain the solutions to problems they have already solved. Once saved from deforestation, a forest needs protection from invasive species. When one generation builds a community center, the next must repair and maintain it. Someone must update the technology that encrypts websites and emails and keeps people safe from surveillance. Nobody can take the commons for granted. Otherwise, all the work on communities, solidarity, culture, innovation, and ecologies risks being undone. For this progress to last, commons stewardship needs support.

### Fiscal hosting in Europe and beyond

OSE is based in Europe but offers fiscal hosting to initiatives around the world. If this vision speaks to you, get in touch. OSE is ready to host your Collective today and would be excited to hear from you. To apply, use the [application form](https://opencollective.com/europe/apply).

# Risk and compliance aspects

Open Source Europe: Grant Eligibility and Risk Assessment Policy

## Introduction

Open Source Europe (OSE) is committed to supporting initiatives that promote positive social change and a more just world. This policy covers grants that a Collective wants to receive through OSE. OSE decides whether to support the proposed funding arrangement. If an application names OSE as recipient or signatory, contact the team before you submit it. OSE must first review and accept its role and commitments. The following sections cover grant eligibility and possible compliance risks linked to terrorism or extremism financing.

***

## Grant eligibility criteria

OSE prioritizes proposals from initiatives that:

* Operate in accordance with the law
* Do not support or glorify terrorist groups
* Show that they manage money responsibly, including transparent record-keeping and reporting

***

## Compliance risk assessment

OSE considers the following factors when it assesses potential compliance risks of a grant proposal. They are in no fixed order of importance:

* Beneficiary impact: Can the initiative show that its work benefits its target communities?
* Public statements: Does the initiative's public messaging avoid promoting violence or extremism?
* Transparency: Does the initiative publish financial statements and reports on its activities?
* Legality: Do the initiative's mission and activities comply with legal frameworks and international law?

***

## Contextual considerations

OSE takes context into account when it evaluates proposals. It carries out due diligence to understand the specific circumstances and actions of the initiative.

***

## Information sources

To assess grant proposals, OSE uses information sources that fit the circumstances of each case. It may use the following sources. They have no fixed ranking, and OSE does not have to check every source for every proposal:

* Initiative websites and reports
* Credible news sources and independent research organizations
* United Nations and human rights organization reports
* Government watchlists and sanctions lists

***

## OSE's decision to support a grant

OSE may accept or decline to support a grant application, or to receive the proposed grant on behalf of a Collective. Do not assume that OSE accepts. The team explains the reasons for its decision to the Collective. It does not commit to a formal written report in every case.

***

## Requesting a review

If OSE declines to support a proposed grant arrangement, the Collective may ask the team to review its decision. OSE does not have a formal appeals procedure.

***

## Policy review and revision

OSE reviews and revises this policy periodically, to make sure it stays effective and in line with best practices.

***

## Conclusion

OSE is committed to balancing the prevention of terrorism financing with support for legitimate initiatives that work toward positive social change. This policy is the framework for that goal.

***

## Need assistance?

For questions or more information about risk and compliance aspects, contact OSE at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Safeguarding policy

## Introduction

Open Source Europe (OSE) is committed to creating a safe and inclusive environment for all staff, volunteers, partners, and beneficiaries. This policy outlines our commitment to safeguarding and sets out procedures for reporting and responding to concerns.

***

## What is safeguarding?

Safeguarding refers to the actions we take to protect people, especially children and vulnerable adults, from harm. This includes protection from:

* Abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, neglect)
* Exploitation
* Neglect
* Discrimination
* Bullying

***

## Our commitment

OSE is committed to:

* Promoting a culture of safety and well-being for everyone involved in our activities
* Sharing safeguarding guidance with staff and volunteers, including how to report concerns and their role in protecting people
* Providing clear procedures for reporting concerns
* Taking all concerns seriously and having the safeguarding leads review them to determine appropriate next steps
* Supporting anyone who has been affected by safeguarding incidents

***

## Who is vulnerable?

Safeguarding applies to everyone, but some people may be more vulnerable to harm. This includes:

* Children
* People with disabilities
* Older adults
* People who are dependent on others

***

## Reporting concerns

Anyone who has a concern about the safety or well-being of someone involved in OSE activities should report it immediately. This applies even if they are not sure about the nature of the concern.

Contact the safeguarding leads listed below to report a concern. OSE does not provide a continuously staffed reporting service or guarantee a response time.

***

## How to report a concern

Concerns can be reported to:

* Safeguarding leads:
  * Ivan Cukeric: <ivan@opencollective.com>
  * Jean-François De Hertogh: <jf@opencollective.com>

If a concern involves one of the safeguarding leads, contact the other lead directly, provided they are not also involved.

Reports can be made in person, by email, or in writing. Information is shared only with those who need it to handle the concern or where disclosure is required by law. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised.

***

## What happens when a concern is reported?

All reported concerns are taken seriously. The safeguarding leads review each report and determine appropriate next steps, including referral to external services or relevant authorities where necessary. OSE does not systematically conduct an internal investigation.

Depending on the circumstances, appropriate action may include:

* Referral to relevant authorities
* Disciplinary action
* Support for the person who raised the concern or the person at risk

***

## Confidentiality

OSE limits the sharing of information about safeguarding concerns to those who need it to handle the concern or where disclosure is required by law. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised.

***

## Support

OSE listens to people affected by safeguarding incidents and directs them toward appropriate support services. OSE does not organize or fund psychological counseling.

***

## Training

OSE shares safeguarding guidance with staff and volunteers, including how to respond to and report concerns. OSE does not currently provide systematic safeguarding training.

***

## Review

This policy will be reviewed regularly to ensure it remains effective.

***

## Need assistance?

For any questions about this policy or safeguarding in general, please contact the safeguarding lead at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Terminology

Open Source Europe (OSE) uses the following terms to describe processes in the Open Collective ecosystem. Use these terms instead of 'user' when you create issues or support requests, because everyone is a user.

## Individuals

Everyone who interacts with the Open Collective platform is an individual. Individuals can take on different roles in the ecosystem:

* Contributor: someone who supports an initiative, with money or in other ways.
* Organizer: an individual who creates or manages an initiative.

## Financial contributors

### Organizational financial contributor

A company or organization that supports an initiative financially, often at a higher tier. People often call these contributors sponsors. They may want benefits such as brand exposure, community goodwill, or tangible perks.

### Individual financial contributor

An individual who supports an initiative financially, with one-time or recurring contributions. They may find initiatives through:

* Open Collective's homepage
* Direct links to a Collective
* Organizer's page

### Expense submitter

An individual who requests payment from an initiative's budget using the expense function. The request can be to get paid back for purchases made for the initiative, or to get paid for completed work.

## Non-financial contributors

### Organizer

An individual who creates or works on an initiative. After they talk with the OSE team, organizers decide whether they create a 'Fund' or a 'Collective'.

### Core contributor

Individuals who are major contributors and represent the Collective on its page as part of the team.

### Collective admin

A type of core contributor with additional permissions that let them:

* Edit the Collective
* Change settings
* Approve expenses
* Make financial contributions to other Collectives
* Receive messages from people trying to contact the Collective

Core contributors aim to make their communities financially sustainable. They use tools such as tiers, goals, and social media sharing. To manage and grow their communities, they create events and send updates.

### Event attendee

Individuals who register to attend a Collective's event. They often arrive through direct links from event organizers.

## Initiatives

Initiatives are accounts for projects or groups that OSE hosts. An initiative can be either a Collective or a Fund. During the application process, the OSE team helps you choose the right account type for your project.

### Collective

A Collective represents a project or group with a mission or purpose. It raises and spends funds transparently to achieve its goals.

## Fiscal hosts

A fiscal host, or sponsor, is a type of organization that lets Collectives handle money without having to legally incorporate. The fiscal host holds a Collective’s funds in its bank account and can generate invoices and receipts for financial contributors. A fiscal host is an umbrella organization for the Collectives it supports.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# About Open Source Europe

Open Source Europe (OSE) is a Belgian association. It is the fiscal host for open source initiatives and works with philanthropic institutions to support regranting around the world.

***

## Service overview

Unlike traditional nonprofits, OSE combines a legal structure with its own digital infrastructure. Together they make the following possible:

* Fiscal hosting for open source projects. OSE gives developers, maintainers, and communities a legal umbrella, so they can operate without creating their own legal entity.
* Grant distribution and fund management. OSE manages funds for foundations and companies that want to support critical open source projects in Europe and beyond.
* Radical transparency. All financial activity is public on the Open Collective platform, which builds trust and accountability in the community.

***

## How hosting works

OSE provides a Belgian nonprofit home for open source projects. OSE uses the Open Collective platform to manage budgets, receive contributions, and process expenses transparently.

For the hosting agreement, see the [Terms of Service](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/).

***

## Who OSE serves

OSE works with the following groups:

* Project maintainers of open source projects that have no legal structure of their own.
* Funders and corporates, such as international companies that want a trusted intermediary to support open source in Europe.
* Developer networks, meaning communities that want fiscal and operational support for their collective activities.

***

## How to work with OSE

You can work with OSE in the following ways:

* Projects can apply for fiscal hosting to start receiving donations and grants legally.
* Funders can support projects and manage their contributions transparently through the funds that OSE hosts.
* Organizations can manage large-scale distributions efficiently, without complex international structures.

***

[Contact the team](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org)

***

## A little history

Open Source Europe grew out of Open Collective Europe's fiscal hosting work. As that work grew, OSE became the home for open source projects and communities. Open Collective Europe Foundation developed its wider philanthropic activities. The OSE hosting agreement still uses the association's name, Open Collective Europe ASBL/vzw.

Today, OSE focuses on helping open source communities receive funding, pay contributors, and manage their projects transparently.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Contributions FAQ

Questions about contributions to the Collectives that Open Source Europe (OSE) hosts.

## How do I cancel a recurring donation, subscription, or payment?

To cancel a recurring donation, subscription, or other ongoing payment, follow the [Open Collective instructions to change or cancel a contribution](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#change-the-amount-payment-method-or-cancel-an-existing-contribution).

## What if a contributor wants their contribution to be anonymous?

Contributors can make an anonymous payment by choosing [incognito](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#profile) when they pick a profile to pay from. If the contributor pays as a [guest](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#contributing-as-a-guest), the name they give still shows. A guest payment only means that the contributor does not have to log in. All Open Collective users can also [separate a public display name from their private legal name](https://opencollective.com/opencollective/updates/new-legal-and-display-name-settings).

## What if a financial contributor cannot or does not want to submit their credit card information online?

If a donor is not comfortable with online credit card transactions, they can send the funds through PayPal or a bank transfer.

## What if a donation does not appear on the Collective's page?

This answer applies when someone says they sent money to your Collective, and also when you sent money yourself. In both cases, [contact OSE](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/contact-us/).

OSE often receives money in its bank account without any sign of where the money should go. This is why the order number in the bank transfer is so important. OSE always searches carefully for the right Collective, but sometimes OSE cannot find it.

OSE keeps unidentified funds pending until it can identify the intended Collective. Once OSE identifies the Collective, OSE can allocate the funds to it. There is no fixed monthly transfer schedule for unidentified funds.

To follow up on a bank transfer, email <home@opensourceeurope.org> with these details:

* Transfer receipt
* Amount
* Date
* Sender's name
* Intended Collective
* Order number, if you have it

Discord is a community space. Do not use it for bank transfer cases or supporting documents.

## What if a financial contributor asks for an invoice before they donate?

OSE can confirm receipt of a donation, but a donation confirmation is not a sales invoice or a value-added tax (VAT) invoice. OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before you commit to sales, invoiced services, or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE. Discuss with OSE whether it can support the arrangement and under what conditions. Do this before you make commitments or receive payment. Acceptance is not guaranteed.

## Can my Collective use outside fundraising platforms?

Open Collective already includes crowdfunding tools and is the usual option. OSE considers external platforms, such as Patreon, Ko-fi, or GoFundMe, case by case. Contact OSE before you set up a campaign to receive funds through OSE. OSE checks payout arrangements, supporting records, and any promised benefits. Compatibility and acceptance are not automatic.

For the GitHub Sponsors route, see [GitHub Sponsors](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/setting-up-github-sponsors/).

## Can my Collective receive earned income that is not a donation?

OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before you commit to sales, invoiced services, or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE. Discuss with OSE whether it can support the arrangement and under what conditions. Do this before you make commitments or receive payment. Acceptance is not guaranteed.

## Can my Collective offer financial contributors something in return for their donation?

Tiers can suggest contribution amounts. If you intend to promise goods, services, advertising, access, or another benefit, contact OSE before you commit or receive funds. OSE checks whether it can support the arrangement. Acceptance is not guaranteed. You can still acknowledge donors, as long as the acknowledgment is optional and not promised as part of a tier.

## Can my Collective offer memberships or accept membership fees?

A symbolic supporter membership gives no rights or benefits. Discuss any proposed membership with benefits with OSE before you commit to it or collect fees. Acceptance is not automatic.

## Can my Collective donate to another hosted Collective?

Transfers to another hosted Collective are different from ordinary external donations. Before you go ahead, get OSE’s approval of the recipient, purpose, and funding conditions. Collectives hosted by OSE [can give to other Collectives](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/collective-to-collective) hosted by OSE. To give to a Collective with another fiscal host, follow [the extra steps for Collectives with different fiscal hosts](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/collective-to-collective#across-different-fiscal-hosts).

## U.S. tax-deductible donations

The established Myriad → OCEF → OSE route supports U.S. tax-deductible giving, subject to applicable tax rules. Contact OSE before payment to organize the right route. For more information, see [U.S. giving](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/what-we-offer/tax-deductible-giving-for-us-donors/).

## Donation refunds

Contact the Collective administrators first. They forward the request to OSE. If they do not respond, contact OSE directly. Contact does not guarantee a refund. For more information, see [Refunds](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/refunds/).

# Fiscal hosting FAQs

## What is a fiscal host?

A fiscal host is an organization that holds funds on behalf of Collectives, so they can operate financially without having to set up a legal entity.

This arrangement is also called fiscal sponsorship. It allows your Collective to:

* Receive and manage donations and grants
* Provide donation confirmations and administer grants
* Handle taxes, bookkeeping, and legal compliance
* Pay expenses approved by your Collective admins

The Open Collective platform provides all the tools to manage these flows transparently.

***

## How do I add a fiscal host to my Collective?

If your Collective does not have a fiscal host yet, follow these steps to add one:

1. Go to your Collective page.
2. Click **Apply to Fiscal Host**.
3. Choose the fiscal host you want, such as Open Source Europe (OSE).

> **Note:** For more information, see [Add a Fiscal Host](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/add-fiscal-host) in the Open Collective documentation.

***

## More information

For more information about hosting with OSE, see [How to apply](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) and the [Terms of Service](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/).

## Moving to another fiscal host

Contact OSE before you leave. You then coordinate with the new fiscal host, settle outstanding expenses, and check the conditions for transferring the balance. Transfers remain subject to the hosting agreement and restrictions on the funds. A change on Open Collective does not automatically change your GitHub Sponsors setup.

## Closing a Collective voluntarily

If the Collective stops operating without moving to another host, settle outstanding expenses first. The Collective then proposes where the remaining balance goes, in line with its purpose. OSE reviews and approves the proposal according to the funding conditions.

For equipment bought with the Collective's budget, the Collective proposes what should happen to it. OSE reviews the proposal and the funding conditions before anything is transferred or disposed of. This process does not decide who owns the equipment, and it does not add a general inventory requirement.

## Inactive Collectives

When a Collective is inactive for a long time, OSE contacts the administrators and sends reminders. The reminders state a deadline to respond and what happens if there is no reply. If there is no response, OSE may end hosting, stop recurring contributions, and reallocate the balance to its general fund or a similar project. OSE takes these steps under the applicable agreement and funding restrictions. There is no universal six-month timeline. This process is separate from the process for unidentified incoming payments.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# General FAQs

## What can I do with an Open Source Europe account?

When your initiative joins Open Source Europe (OSE), it can:

* Collect recurring or one-off donations
* Apply for subsidies or grants
* Pay invoices and reimburse expenses
* Offer full budget transparency to your community
* Operate without creating your own legal entity
* Pay service providers on compliant invoices, including through workers’ cooperatives
* Reimburse eligible volunteer expenses

***

## What am I not allowed to do?

To comply with the legal and charitable framework of OSE, you may not:

* Issue invoices or sign documents in the name of OSE. Any specific contract that needs OSE’s signature must be discussed and accepted beforehand. Do not use OSE’s legal name or VAT number to have supplier invoices issued for your Collective.
* Use funds to influence legislation or politics (lobbying).
* Support or engage in illegal activity.
* Use funds for personal profit.
* Have another fiscal host at the same time. Technical or community affiliations may be accepted after review.
* Spend funds on purposes outside your initiative’s mission. If you do, they must be reimbursed.

***

## Why should I use Open Collective?

OSE uses the Open Collective platform to make financial management simpler and more transparent.

Benefits include:

* Easy collection of recurring or one-off contributions
* Simple spending: submit a receipt or invoice → approve → paid
* Automatic and public budget tracking
* Shared financial visibility, which builds collaboration and trust

> OSE believes that transparency makes communities more resilient and democratic.

***

## How is Open Source Europe different?

OSE differs in these ways:

* Designed for collaborative communities, as well as for campaigns or individuals
* Open source, with built-in transparency (no hidden ledgers)
* Fiscal hosting as a service, with a nonprofit legal framework
* Based in Europe, but globally connected

***

## How much does it cost?

The following table lists the current OSE hosting fees:

| Contribution type                                                 | OSE fee |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| Ordinary online crowdfunding donations by card (Stripe) or PayPal | 8%      |
| Incoming bank transfers                                           | 10%     |
| Grants and public subsidies                                       | 10%     |
| Tax-deductible donations through the supported intermediary route | 10%     |
| GitHub Sponsors                                                   | 10%     |

For ordinary card and PayPal donations, OSE calculates the 8% hosting fee on the donation amount before payment processing fees. For example, a €20 donation has a €1.60 OSE hosting fee. Payment processing fees are separate and also reduce the amount available to the Collective. The amount of these fees can vary.

The 10% OSE hosting fee applies to incoming bank transfers, grants and public subsidies, donations through Myriad → OCEF → OSE, and GitHub Sponsors. OSE calculates this fee on each amount that it actually receives, after any fees deducted before the money reaches OSE.

Currency conversion services or intermediaries may have additional costs. Contact OSE to confirm the costs applicable to a specific route. This page gives no combined fee rate.

These are the current rates. This page does not introduce any fee reduction.

***

## Can my Collective get a discount?

OSE often gets requests for fee reductions and understands why. Many initiatives bring in funds that they already raised, and OSE knows how tight nonprofit budgets can be.

OSE already keeps its standard fees as low as possible. The fees cover the real costs of:

* Legal and administrative management
* Risk and compliance
* Payments, reports, and support over time

> **Caution:** The standard OSE hosting fees apply. OSE does not offer hosting fee discounts or waivers.

***

## What if I want to become my own fiscal host someday?

You can use OSE as your fiscal host for as long as you need it and remain eligible.

* You can ask to end fiscal hosting, following the notice and remaining-balance rules in your [hosting agreement](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/).
* If you plan to manage your own structure, OSE can help you prepare.
* The [Open Collective platform](https://opencollective.com/) also supports organizations that wish to become fiscal hosts themselves.

***

## How long does it take to get started?

* The application process only takes a few minutes.
* OSE might contact you with a few follow-up questions.
* Once your application is accepted, you can start receiving donations right away.

> **Note:** The application and the acceptance are separate steps. See [How to apply](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) for the review process and indicative response time. OSE may ask for more information before acceptance.

***

## Is there a minimum required budget?

No. OSE does not require a minimum balance to host your initiative.

Since our fees are taken as a percentage of incoming contributions, you can start small and grow as your initiative develops.

## Paying collaborators

Collectives can pay service providers against a compliant invoice, including through a workers’ cooperative. Agree the work, price, and dates with the Collective and submit the invoice through Open Collective for review. OSE does not provide a standard employment or payroll service. If an arrangement needs OSE to sign a specific contract, discuss the arrangement with OSE and get its acceptance first.

## Discounts and nonprofit benefits

OSE may support a request or provide an attestation on a case-by-case basis. Hosting does not automatically qualify a Collective for every nonprofit discount or benefit. Each supplier sets its own eligibility criteria. OSE cannot guarantee acceptance.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Application Questions

## Prepare Your Answers Before Applying

Prepare your answers to the following questions before you apply to Open Source Europe (OSE). This makes the application faster and easier, and helps you explain the purpose of your initiative.

***

## Required Information

* **Location:** Give the city and country where your initiative is mainly based. OSE hosts initiatives all over the world, but knowing your location helps us support you better.
* **Your Name and Email Address:** Give your full name and a valid email address where we can contact you.
* **Collective Name:** Choose a unique name for your collective that describes it.
* **Website and/or Social Media Links:** Share links that show your initiative’s activities and online presence.
* **Unique URL:** You can choose a unique URL for your collective’s page on the Open Collective platform.
* **Administrators:** One administrator is enough, and two are recommended for shared management and continuity. OSE must know the administrators' real identities. A public pseudonym is allowed. Administrators have full permissions to manage the Collective’s settings and finances.

***

## Application Questions

Prepare short answers (about 250 characters) to the following questions:

1. **Duration:** How long has your collective been operating?
2. **Fundraising to Date:** If you’ve started fundraising, how much have you raised so far?
3. **Fundraising Goals:** What is your target fundraising amount?
4. **Funding Sources:** Who do you anticipate will fund your initiative?
5. **Collective Activities:** Briefly describe what your collective does.
6. **Mission Alignment:** Explain how your collective furthers one or more of OSE’s mission impact areas.

***

## Tips for a Successful Application

* Keep your answers clear and to the point.
* Show how your initiative contributes to the public good and fits OSE’s mission.
* Include links to your work, such as project websites, social media pages or articles, to support your application.
* Check your answers for clarity and completeness before you submit your application.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have questions or need help with the application process, [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Eligibility

## Who Can Apply to Be Hosted by Open Source Europe?

Open Source Europe (OSE) welcomes initiatives from around the world that align with our mission and values. OSE supports open source projects and communities. Your application should explain how your activities contribute to open source. OSE can accept an initiative before it publishes its first code or other open resources. OSE first reviews the initiative and its commitments to openness.

***

## Eligibility Criteria

To be eligible for fiscal hosting by OSE, your initiative must:

* Align with OSE's mission and impact areas. Your activities should be charitable and aim to benefit the public.
* Be non-profit. Profits must not be distributed to members. For the types of contributions accepted through OSE, including the rules on membership benefits and other counterparty benefits, see [Contributions FAQ](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/faq/contributions-faq/).
* Have no separate legal entity, for ordinary fiscal hosting. Initiatives with their own legal status, such as registered NGOs, are not eligible for ordinary fiscal hosting. They can set up a Fund with OSE for a specific programme. OSE must first review and agree to the programme and how the Fund will operate. Contact OSE to discuss the arrangement. OSE does not accept it automatically.
* Have at least one administrator. One is enough, and two are recommended for shared management and continuity. OSE must know the administrators' real identities. A public pseudonym is allowed.
* Keep to appropriate content standards. Content that promotes violence, hate speech, pornography, or any other material considered inappropriate or offensive is not permitted.

***

## Global Reach

OSE welcomes applications from around the world. The team assesses which hosting and payment arrangements are available for each application. A project's location alone does not guarantee that hosting or payments will be possible.

***

## Not Required

OSE aims to lower barriers for initiatives with impact, so we do not require:

* Application fees
* A minimum budget balance
* A minimum annual fundraising amount
* A fixed duration of commitment
* Complex reporting requirements as a general condition of hosting. OSE recommends an annual update on your Collective page. Reporting requirements in a specific funding arrangement or agreement still apply.

***

## Important Considerations

* OSE administers funds on behalf of your initiative under the hosting agreement. If you move to another host or close, contact OSE to agree how outstanding expenses and the remaining balance are handled under the applicable agreement and funding restrictions.
* OSE assesses possible compliance risks of initiatives. It checks that initiatives align with legal frameworks and avoid activities that could be linked to terrorism or extremism financing.

***

## Ready to Apply?

If your initiative meets the criteria above, follow our [How to Apply](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) guide to start your application.

If you have questions, [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Affiliation with another organisation

OSE does not accept fiscal hosting at the same time as another host. OSE may accept a technical or community affiliation with another organisation after review. Affiliation alone does not mean fiscal hosting.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# How to apply

Use this guide to prepare and submit a hosting application, and to learn how OSE reviews it.

## Start here

1. Read the [eligibility criteria](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/eligibility/), [hosting fees](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/faq/general-faqs/#how-much-does-it-cost) and [application questions](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/application-questions/).
2. Prepare your project details and at least one administrator. We recommend two.
3. Follow the application process below, then complete the supplementary form that OSE provides.

Next, OSE aims to give a first response within seven business days after it receives the completed supplementary form. This is a target for the response, not a deadline for acceptance. After acceptance, continue with [your first steps](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/basics/).

## Join Open Source Europe in just a few steps

Applying to be hosted by Open Source Europe (OSE) is simple and usually takes a few minutes. After OSE accepts you, you can receive contributions and manage your initiative in the open on the Open Collective platform.

***

## Before You Apply

Check that your initiative meets these criteria:

* It aligns with OSE's mission and impact areas. Your activities should be charitable and aim to benefit the public.
* It has at least one administrator. One is enough, and two are recommended for shared management and continuity. OSE must know the administrators' real identities. A public pseudonym is allowed.
* For ordinary fiscal hosting, it has no legal entity of its own. An existing legal entity can instead discuss a Fund for a specific programme with OSE. This depends on OSE's review and agreement on the programme and on how the Fund will operate.
* It can be based anywhere in the world, not only in Europe.

Also read our [Terms of Cooperation](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) and [Community Guidelines](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/community-guidelines/).

***

## Application Process

1. Go to the [Open Source Europe profile](https://opencollective.com/europe) and click "Apply".
2. Choose your collective type:
   * If you are new to the Open Collective platform, select "Create New Collective".
   * If you already have a collective, choose it from the list.
3. Complete the application form. Give information about your initiative, including:
   * Location
   * Name and email address
   * Collective name
   * Website and/or social media links
   * Brief description of your collective's activities
   * Explanation of how your collective furthers OSE's mission impact areas
4. Add at least one administrator. Two are recommended for shared management and continuity.
5. Review your information, accept the terms of service and submit your application.

You can edit all this information later, so it does not need to be perfect.

***

## After Submission

To complete the review, the team gives you a supplementary application form. Do not wait for an automatic email.

We aim to give a first response within seven business days of receiving your completed supplementary form. The review may take longer if we need more information. This does not guarantee acceptance, or that the review ends within seven days.

After acceptance, you can start to receive contributions. Welcome calls happen only occasionally and are not a standard onboarding step. Contributions can start without waiting for a call.

***

## Transitioning from Another Fiscal Host

If you are moving from another fiscal host:

* If you use the Open Collective platform, the move is fairly simple.
* If you do not use the Open Collective platform, the process depends on what your current organization requires. Usually, they can transfer your funds to OSE, and you can start quickly.

Tell both OSE and your current fiscal host about your plans before you apply, so that the move goes smoothly.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have questions or need help with the application process, [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

# Ask OSE from your AI tools

The Open Source Europe (OSE) knowledge base searches these docs and answers questions about OSE with cited sources. You can ask it in the chat at Ask OSE (link removed: /ask/), or connect it to your own AI assistant. The knowledge base then runs on your own computer, so OSE does not see your questions.

All three ways start the knowledge base with `uvx`, so install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) first.

## Use it as an MCP server

Add the server to any Model Context Protocol (MCP) client, such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Claude Desktop. In Claude Code, run the following command:

```bash
claude mcp add ose-knowledge -- uvx ose-knowledge-mcp
```

For another client, add the following JSON to the client's configuration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ose-knowledge": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["ose-knowledge-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

The version is fixed, so you always get a known build. Each OSE release updates the version on this page.

## Use it as a Claude Code plugin

The plugin adds the MCP server, an `ose-researcher` agent, and an `ask-about-ose` skill. The skill sends your OSE questions to the agent. You can also call the skill as `/ose-knowledge:ask-about-ose`.

In Claude Code, run the following commands to install the plugin:

```text
/plugin marketplace add opensourceeurope/ose-ai
/plugin install ose-knowledge@ose-ai
```

## Use it as a Codex plugin

The same plugin installs in Codex with the MCP server and the `ask-about-ose` skill. Codex does not load the `ose-researcher` agent, so the skill searches the knowledge base itself.

The following command adds the plugin marketplace to Codex:

```bash
codex plugin marketplace add opensourceeurope/ose-ai
```

Then run `/plugins` in Codex, install `ose-knowledge`, and start a new session. To install from the terminal instead, run `codex plugin add ose-knowledge@ose-ai` and start a new session.

## Give the docs to any AI tool

An AI tool that reads web pages can also use the docs without the knowledge base. Give the tool the address of one of these files:

- [llms.txt](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/llms.txt) lists the pages of the website and the docs, with a short description of each.
- [llms-full.txt](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/llms-full.txt) holds the text of every docs page in one file, with the address of each page.
- Each docs page also has a Markdown copy. Replace the slash at the end of its address with `.md`, for example [basics.md](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/basics.md).

llms.txt and llms-full.txt follow the [llms.txt format](https://llmstxt.org).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Deciding on how to use your money

This guide explains how to use funds for your initiative on Open Source Europe (OSE).

This guide is based on an Open Source Collective workshop led by Sumana Harihareswara of Changeset Consulting in January 2022. It helped open source software projects hosted on Open Collective decide how to use the money they had already raised. OSE adapted the workshop content to the cases that OSE sees. All examples are in euros (EUR).

## Why you should (or shouldn't) spend your money

The following sections list reasons to spend and reasons to save.

### Reasons to spend

Spending money can help your project in these ways:

* Advance your project. Pay for tasks, chores, and infrastructure improvements that are hard to do with volunteer labor alone.
* Attract more donors. When you spend money, donors see that you use their contributions well.
* Experiment and learn. Money for pilot projects or services can help you try new approaches and gives you more flexibility.
* Boost morale. Small purchases of merchandise (stickers, awards, and t-shirts) can help contributors stay and can improve team morale.

Agree together on rules for spending decisions that suit your Collective's budget. Make clear who can approve expenses and which decisions need a wider discussion. These internal rules do not replace OSE's expense checks or the conditions attached to your funding.

### Reasons to save

Keep money in reserve for these reasons:

* Specific activities. Save up for large expenses, such as hiring contractors.
* Self-insurance. Keep funds to cover possible risks, such as unexpected hosting costs or legal expenses.
* Budgeting. Make a budget that sets funds aside for self-insurance and for future activities. Then you know clearly how much you can spend.

## Driver and supporter/protector activities

Activities and expenses fall into three groups:

* Drivers are activities that directly advance your mission, for example software development.
* Supporters are infrastructure activities and purchases that support drivers, for example organizing conferences or buying laptops.
* Protectors are activities or expenses that reduce risks, for example legal fees or code of conduct workshops.

The following diagram shows the money and resources that go into a project and come out of it.

[Image removed: Diagram of money and resources flowing into a project from creators, individual users, platforms, and organizational users, and out to platforms and services, labor, convenings and travel, equipment and supplies, and outgoing donations and grants]

*Money and resources that go into a project, and what comes out of it*

In the diagram, labor for software development is a driver, because writing the software directly advances the mission of making and improving the open source project. A conference where the contributors can meet to improve and speed up their work is a supporter activity. A new laptop for a contributor to use is a supporter purchase.

## Advancing your goals and roadmap

Consider what's on your roadmap and how you can spend to support it.

If your project has no clear goals or written roadmap, you can still spend money in the following ways:

* Pay consultants who help you create a roadmap.
* Upgrade the hardware of your team's development environment.
* Reimburse volunteers. Volunteers can ask for reimbursement of their actual expenses, with the required supporting documents. OSE may consider a separate volunteer allowance arrangement, but OSE must review and accept the arrangement beforehand. OSE does not accept such an arrangement automatically.

If you have a roadmap, pay new contractors or services to take repetitive tasks off your existing volunteers.

### Specific spending examples

Collectives spend money on items such as these:

* Independent contractors
* Volunteer reimbursements
* Professional education and tools
* Travel expenses for meetups
* Logo design and merchandise
* Co-working space
* Virtual assistant services

### Hiring contractors

You can hire collaborators for your Collective as contractors. You can choose who to hire informally or through a public job posting. For more information, see [the invoicing options](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/).

### Using bounties cautiously

Patch bounty programs can encourage specific development work. They may also make people compete rather than cooperate. Use bounties for tasks that volunteers do not want to do or do not have the skills for. OSE treats bounty payments as payments for services: each bounty payment needs a compliant invoice, and the usual payment rules apply.

## Decision-making and governance

Open Collective's expense documentation says:

> **Note:** "The decision is up to you as a project. Some projects are informal, and any Core Contributor can approve any expense. Others have a formal decision-making or budgeting process, or only pay expenses for specific things. We advise you to have a discussion with your collaborators and agree on guidelines for approving expenses."

Also read the Open Collective documentation on [budget](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/budget) and [expense policies](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/collective-settings/expense-policy), and the blog post ["Ten ways to make decisions about money"](https://blog.opencollective.com/ten-ways-to-make-decisions-about-money/).

### Common concerns

Two concerns come up often:

* OSE cannot advise you on the legal or tax obligations of your members or collaborators. OSE recommends that you contact a legal or tax specialist in their country of residence. For general guidance, use this documentation or contact OSE at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.
* If people disagree, act in good faith and support decisions made by the group. Clear policies and consistent practices help a lot.

People may have reasonable concerns about what you spent, and why and how you spent it. If you are not sure how to prevent or answer those concerns, you have two main options:

* *Intense up-front transparency*: publish the details of your decisions openly. Tell contributors and observers about possible expenses in advance, make clear who decides, and offer a public comment period before approval. Do this every time, and use Open Collective's tools to keep the records available for later review. This approach is fairly easy if you manage all expenses through Open Collective invoices.
* *Post-decision accountability*: do not offer a public comment period before the decision. Instead, run a clear private comment period among the people who decide. Then answer for past expenses: anyone who wants to can ask for details about a specific expense. This approach lets you make more decisions privately, and you can give some details privately when people ask. Your payees, or the people you answer, may publish details on their own.

## OSE’s role in conflicts

Collectives manage their internal conflicts. OSE intervenes if a situation affects funds or hosting conditions, but does not promise mediation. If you suspect misuse of funds, or have concerns about administrators, contact OSE privately. You do not have to go through those administrators.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Basics

This page is your starting point after Open Source Europe (OSE) accepts your Collective. Work through the essentials, then use the relevant guide for each transaction.

## Your first steps

1. Check your public profile and contacts. Use the platform's [Quick Start Guide](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/quick-start-guide). Keep administrator access and the main contact up to date, and notify OSE of changes.
2. Choose how to receive funds. Start with [donations and funding routes](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/). You can receive contributions without waiting for a welcome call.
3. Agree how your Collective makes spending decisions. Read [budget decisions](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/guides/deciding-on-how-to-use-your-money/).
4. Prepare your first payment. Use [Pay and get reimbursed](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/). Your Collective must receive the funds before payment, and the funds must be available.
5. Keep the community informed. Use Updates and review the responsibilities on this page.

Some steps need OSE's agreement first. Contact the OSE team before any of these steps:

* A grant application that names OSE as recipient or signatory
* A specific contract that OSE would sign
* A proposed commercial arrangement

The section "Top five things to remember" gives the details.

## Welcome to Open Source Europe

Once OSE approves your hosting application, you can start to manage your Collective on the Open Collective platform right away.

***

## Top five things to remember

The following points apply to every Collective that OSE hosts:

* If an arrangement requires OSE to sign a specific contract, discuss the contract with OSE and get OSE's acceptance first.
* If a grant application names OSE as recipient or signatory, contact the OSE team before you submit the application. The team can then review and accept OSE's role and commitments.
* Use the Updates feature to keep your community informed. OSE recommends at least one update per year. This recommendation is not a general hosting obligation. Reporting requirements in a funding arrangement or applicable agreement still apply.
* For expenses, follow the [expense guide](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/) for documents, review, and payment.
* OSE mainly supports donations and grants. Before you commit to sales, invoiced services, or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE. Discuss whether OSE can support the arrangement, and under what conditions. Do this before you receive any payment. OSE does not guarantee acceptance.

***

## Understanding Open Collective

Open Collective is the platform that OSE operates on. It provides tools to budget transparently, customize a Collective profile, set up tiers and goals, and more.

For an overview of the Open Collective platform, see its [documentation](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/about/documentation). It explains the features you can use.

Its [Quick Start Guide](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/quick-start-guide) is another good place to start.

***

## Budget management of your Collective

These docs have one page about how to receive funds and one about how to submit expenses. You can share these pages with the contributors and members of your Collective.

When OSE hosts your Collective, your Collective joins a community of hundreds of initiatives. They use the same tools to manage their independent projects. This setup needs little attention, but it does need some to work properly.

Read the Open Collective guidelines on [donations](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/raising-money) and [expenses](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses). If you have questions or doubts, contact OSE at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

***

## Important notes

The following points cover your own obligations:

* You must understand and fulfill all of your tax obligations. If you’re not sure whether you need to charge or pay tax, OSE encourages you to ask a tax professional. OSE can’t give tax advice.
* The OSE [Terms of Service](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) give details about your responsibilities and OSE's policies.

***

## Get help

If you have questions or need help, [contact OSE](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Keep your contacts up to date

When administrators or the main contact change, update access on Open Collective and notify OSE so the team can keep supporting you without a break.

## Optional welcome call

Welcome calls happen only occasionally and are not a standard step. Contributions can start after acceptance without waiting for a call. See [How to apply](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Expenses and getting paid: frequently asked questions

For the steps from planning a purchase to payment, start with the [expense guide](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/). This page answers specific payment questions.

## How does paying people work?

Submit an expense through the Collective’s page. The Collective and Open Source Europe (OSE) review expenses. If the sole administrator requests their own reimbursement, OSE can check the supporting documents and pay without a second approver on the Collective side.

OSE aims to start the payment within seven business days. These days count from when the expense is complete and approved, and the Collective has received the necessary funds and has them available. Bank processing time comes on top. The seven days are a target, not a guaranteed date of receipt.

***

## How do I get paid / reimbursed / receive my grant money?

Go to your Collective's page and click **Submit Expense**. Log in or create an account. Then upload a valid receipt or invoice.

> **Note:** For more information, see [How to submit an expense](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses) in the Open Collective docs.

***

## Invoice or reimbursement: which one do I need?

Choose the expense type that matches your situation:

* If you paid with your own money, use a reimbursement. You need a receipt that shows the vendor's name, address, and tax ID. Order confirmations are not valid receipts.
* When you request payment for services, use an invoice. You need a formal invoice with contact details, tax information, and a description of the services.

> **Note:** For more information, see [Invoices or reimbursements?](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/).

***

## Can we pay people for their time?

Collectives can pay service providers against a compliant invoice. This includes payment through a workers’ cooperative. Agree the work, price, and dates with the Collective. Then submit the invoice through Open Collective for review. OSE does not provide a standard employment or payroll service. If an arrangement requires OSE to sign a specific contract, OSE must discuss and accept it beforehand.

## Which documents are needed?

Address invoices to the Collective or the person who placed the order. OSE acts only as the payer for these purchases. Collectives must not ask for invoices in OSE’s legal name or with OSE's value-added tax (VAT) number.

Reimbursements require an invoice or receipt. A bank statement alone is not enough. For more information, see the [expense guide](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/) and [Invoices or reimbursements?](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/).

***

## Can I donate part of my Collective’s budget to a charity?

A Collective can make ordinary external donations to identified nonprofit organizations. OSE must first review and approve the beneficiary, purpose, and funding conditions. Contact OSE before you make a commitment or request payment. Other types of recipient require a specific assessment, and OSE does not promise to accept them. Once OSE has confirmed the arrangement, the beneficiary submits the request with the following documents:

* A donation request letter, signed by one of the beneficiary's administrators, that states the amount and purpose of the donation
* Incorporation document of the beneficiary
* Bank identification details of the beneficiary

> **Danger:** A donation is not the same as a payment for goods or services. A donation can still come with limits on how the money is used, and with reporting obligations. If the donation comes with a promised benefit or service in return, discuss the arrangement with OSE before you go ahead.

***

## Are receipts and invoices public?

The public budget shows an expense’s title, amount, and public display name. Do not put sensitive information in the title. The public cannot see attached receipts, detailed descriptions, or payment details. Who can see these details depends on the information and the platform permissions. Access is not limited to OSE staff. For more information, see [Open Collective’s reimbursement privacy guidance](https://documentation.opencollective.com/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses/submitting-a-reimbursement) and [expense-submission guidance](https://documentation.opencollective.com/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses).

***

## Need help?

Use the comments on the expense for routine questions and follow-up. Expense comments are not public. The expense submitter, the Collective’s administrators, and the fiscal host’s administrators can see them. For sensitive information that the Collective’s administrators should not see, email OSE directly at <home@opensourceeurope.org>. For more information, see [Open Collective’s expense-comment guidance](https://documentation.opencollective.com/expenses-and-getting-paid/editing-an-expense).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Expenses

Prepare a payment from your Collective's budget. Start by choosing the situation that matches your request.

## Choose your payment

| Your situation                                             | Where to start                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| You have already paid for something for the Collective     | [Prepare a reimbursement](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/#prepare-a-reimbursement)      |
| You need to pay a supplier for goods or services          | [Prepare an invoice](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/#prepare-an-invoice)                |
| The payment is a donation or grant to another organization | [Ask Open Source Europe (OSE) about an outgoing grant or donation](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/request-a-grant-for-nonprofits-only/) |

## Before you submit

Check the following points before you submit an expense:

* Have the invoice or receipt and the payment details ready. A bank statement alone is not enough for a reimbursement.
* Check that the Collective has received the funds you need and that the funds are available.
* For supplier invoices, use the name of the Collective or of the person who placed the order. Do not use OSE's legal name or value-added tax (VAT) number.
* If you are not sure an expense is eligible, ask OSE before you spend. If OSE must sign a specific contract, agree the contract with OSE in advance.

When you are ready, go to Submission process. If you have already submitted, read Approval workflow, or use the expense comments for routine follow-up. Send sensitive information privately.

The payment target is seven business days once the expense is complete and approved and funds are available. Bank processing time comes on top of this target. The target is not a guaranteed date of receipt.

## About the expense process

OSE designed the expense process to be transparent and simple. You can use it to reimburse a team member or to pay a service provider. The process keeps spending accountable and in line with fiscal regulations.

***

## Before spending and requesting reimbursement

OSE does not ask for advance approval of every ordinary expense. If you are not sure an expense is eligible, contact OSE before you spend. OSE still reviews each reimbursement. If an arrangement needs OSE to sign a specific contract, OSE must discuss and accept it in advance.

If someone cannot pay the cost first, OSE can pay the supplier directly on a compliant invoice. OSE does not provide advances to individuals. OSE may pay a supplier deposit before delivery or completion. OSE must first review and agree to the documents and conditions, and the funds must be available.

***

## Types of expenses

You can submit two main types of expenses:

### Reimbursements

Use a reimbursement when someone has paid for goods or services for the Collective with their own money.

Add fiscal receipts that show the following details:

* Vendor's name, address, and tax reference
* Transaction date
* Description of items or services
* Amount paid

> **Caution:** Order confirmations, proforma invoices, or bank statements are not valid receipts. For more information, see [How to submit a reimbursement](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/reimbursement).

### Invoices

Use an invoice to pay people or organizations for services they provided.

Add an invoice that shows the following details:

* Unique invoice number
* Service provider's full details (name, address, and tax ID)
* Detailed description of services
* Applicable tax rate and amount
* Name of the Collective or of the person who placed the order, as the addressee

> **Danger:** Address invoices to the Collective or the person who placed the order. OSE acts only as the payer for these purchases. Collectives must not ask for invoices in OSE’s legal name or with OSE's VAT number. For more information, see [How to submit an invoice](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/invoices).

***

## Supporting documents and timing of submission

OSE refuses reimbursement without an invoice or receipt. A bank statement alone is not enough. Durable equipment needs the usual supporting documents. As a rule, OSE does not ask for an extra inventory. Specific funding or agreement requirements still apply.

There is no general fixed deadline to submit a reimbursement. You must still meet the deadlines in a funding agreement or for a closure. OSE can reimburse expenses from before it accepted the Collective. OSE first reviews the connection of these expenses to the project, the documents, and the funding conditions, and the funds must be available.

***

## Paying service providers

Collectives can pay service providers against a compliant invoice, including through a workers’ cooperative. Agree the work, price, and dates with the Collective. Then submit the invoice through Open Collective for review. OSE does not provide a standard employment or payroll service. If an arrangement requires OSE to sign a specific contract, OSE must discuss and accept it beforehand.

***

## Submission process

Follow these steps to submit an expense:

1. Go to your Collective's page and click **Submit Expense**.
2. Choose the expense type: **Reimbursement** or **Invoice**.
3. Fill in the required details and upload the documents.
4. Select a payout method, such as PayPal or a bank transfer through Wise.
5. Submit the expense for approval.

> **Note:** OSE aims to start the payment within seven business days. The expense must be complete and approved. The Collective must have received the funds, and the funds must be available. Bank processing time comes on top of these seven days. The seven days are a target, not a guaranteed date of receipt.

***

## Approval workflow

The Collective and OSE review expenses. If the only administrator asks for their own reimbursement, OSE can check the supporting documents and pay without a second approver from the Collective.

OSE checks the documents before payment. OSE may reject incomplete or non-compliant expenses. A promised donation or grant is not an available balance. The Collective must receive the funds, and the funds must be available, before OSE pays.

***

## Payment methods

OSE supports the following payout methods:

* PayPal, with an active and verified account
* Bank transfer through Wise, with international bank details

> **Danger:** Make sure the payout details match the expense documents, or the payment may be delayed.

***

## Compliance and best practices

Follow these practices when you submit an expense:

* Keep sensitive information out of the expense title. The public can see an expense's title, amount, and public display name. The public cannot see supporting documents and payment details.
* Double-check amounts, details, and receipts before you submit.
* Use expense comments for routine questions and follow-up. Comments are not public. The expense submitter, the Collective's administrators, and the fiscal host's administrators can see them. For sensitive information that the Collective's administrators should not see, email <home@opensourceeurope.org> directly.

> **Note:** For help, email OSE at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

***

## Learn more

The following pages have more information about expenses:

* [Overview: How to submit expenses](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses)
* [Expenses in the ledger, in the Open Collective docs](https://docs.opencollective.com/open-collective-docs/product/ledger/expenses-in-the-ledger)
* [Expenses and getting paid: frequently asked questions](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/expenses-and-getting-paid-faqs/)
* [Outgoing grants and donations](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/request-a-grant-for-nonprofits-only/)


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Invoices or reimbursements?

Choose the request type before you submit an expense. Use **Reimbursement** if you have already paid. Use **Invoice** when a supplier asks for payment for goods or services.

## Submit your request

1. Choose the matching document checklist on this page: Prepare an invoice or Prepare a reimbursement.
2. Open your Collective on Open Collective and choose **Submit Expense**.
3. Select the type, complete the details, attach the supporting document, and choose the payout method.
4. Submit the expense for review by the Collective and Open Source Europe (OSE). Follow the [approval and payment guidance](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/#approval-workflow).

If someone cannot pay the cost first, OSE can pay the supplier directly on a compliant invoice. OSE does not provide advances to individuals. OSE pays only after a review, and only when the funds are available.

For a donation or grant to another organization, use the [outgoing grants guide](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/request-a-grant-for-nonprofits-only/). Do not treat a donation or grant as a supplier invoice.

## The difference between the two types

When you submit an expense to your Collective, choose the correct type.

## Prepare an invoice

Use an invoice to request payment for services or goods you have provided.

An invoice has the following characteristics:

* Freelancers, contractors, and companies submit invoices.
* Invoices pay for goods or services, including a supplier deposit. For a deposit, OSE must first review and agree to the documents and conditions in advance, and the funds must be available.
* A formal invoice needs the following details:
  * Unique invoice number
  * Full identification (name, address, and tax or company number)
  * Detailed description of the service or goods
  * Applicable tax rate and amount. If the tax rate is zero, put a legal reference for the exemption on the invoice itself (for example, value-added tax (VAT) exemption according to article YY of law XX).
  * Addressed to the Collective or the person who placed the order, with the appropriate recipient details

> **Danger:** Address invoices to the Collective or the person who placed the order. OSE acts only as the payer for these purchases. Collectives must not ask for invoices in OSE’s legal name or with OSE's VAT number.

***

## Prepare a reimbursement

Use a reimbursement when you have paid for something for the Collective with your own money and want the money back.

A reimbursement has the following characteristics:

* Members or contributors of the Collective submit reimbursements.
* Reimbursements pay back purchases made for the Collective.
* A reimbursement needs a valid receipt from the provider that shows:
  * Vendor's name and address
  * Transaction date
  * Description of items or services
  * Amount paid

> **Caution:** Order confirmations, proforma invoices, and bank or PayPal statements are not valid receipts.

***

## Special cases

If you ask for reimbursement of only part of a receipt, highlight the relevant items on the document itself.

> **Tip:** Sometimes the breakdown is not obvious, such as a percentage or a split. In that case, explain the calculation clearly in your request and attach the supporting receipt. OSE may ask for clarification. As a rule, OSE does not require a signed and dated note.

***

## Learn more

The following Open Collective pages have more explanations and tutorials:

* [Overview: Submitting expenses](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses)
* [Expenses: General guidance](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/expenses)

***

## Need help?

If you have questions, [contact OSE](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Documents and review

OSE refuses reimbursement without an invoice or receipt. A bank statement alone is not enough. For the rules on prior spending, submission timing, available funds, and payment targets, see [Expenses](https://www.opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/).
